scoreNote: Strong (5): grants that self-set goals are a humane corrective to empty comparison, then argues 'primarily' overreaches because goals can be unworthy and success has an outward, ethical dimension; nuanced and well argued.

sentences.text: One runner is thrilled to finish a race she trained years for; another, far faster, is bitter at coming second — which of them has succeeded?
The statement answers by making success personal, holding that true success can be measured primarily in terms of the goals one sets for oneself.

Measuring success against one's own goals is a real and valuable corrective to empty comparison, but the word primarily claims too much, since the worth of one's goals, and the effect of one's success on others, also belong to any honest measure.

sections.role: Body — Self-set goals are a fair measure

sentences.text: The statement rightly resists measuring everyone by a single external yardstick.
People begin from different circumstances and want different things, so judging them all by the same standard of wealth or fame is both unfair and shallow.
A person who overcomes great obstacles to reach a modest goal has succeeded more truly than one who inherits an easy triumph, even if the world ranks them otherwise.
Setting and reaching one's own goals also reflects autonomy and self-knowledge, measuring success by growth and effort rather than by accident of birth or luck.
As a guard against hollow comparison, the statement holds much wisdom.

sections.role: Body — But goals can be unworthy

sentences.text: However, to make personal goals the primary measure ignores that the goals themselves can be poor.
A person may set goals that are trivial, far beneath her potential, or even wicked, and reaching them is no true success at all.
A criminal who achieves every aim he sets has, by the statement's logic, succeeded, which shows that merely hitting one's targets cannot by itself make success genuine.
If we can succeed simply by aiming low and clearing the bar we set for ourselves, then success becomes too easy and too empty to mean much.
A goal set deliberately low is not a triumph to celebrate but a horizon needlessly shrunk.
What we aim at matters as much as whether we reach it, so goals cannot be the whole measure.

sections.role: Body — Success has an outward dimension

sentences.text: Moreover, success is not a purely private affair.
How our achievements affect others — whether they help or harm, build or exploit — belongs to any true measure of success, however well they satisfy our own goals.
A life counted successful by its own goals but ruinous to everyone around it is not a model of success but a warning, and we sense this immediately.
The fullest success unites worthy goals, real achievement, and a positive effect on the world, none of which the statement's inward measure captures on its own.
Personal goals are one dimension of success, but worth and consequence are others the statement leaves out.
In conclusion, the statement is right that self-set goals are a meaningful and humane measure of success, but wrong to make them the primary one.

True success depends not only on whether we reach the goals we set, but on whether those goals are worthy and whether our achievement does good in the world, so personal goals are an essential part of the measure rather than the whole of it.
Measure yourself by your own goals, but choose goals worth measuring up to.
